title: Lunar Hatching Patterns in Intertidal Fish Species From the Temperate Coast of Central Chile
content:
ABSTRACT

Understanding the timing of larval hatching and recruitment is essential for elucidating population replenishment processes in marine fishes with complex life cycles. In this study, we examined the relationship between lunar cycles and hatching patterns of two ecologically important intertidal fish species with contrasting life-history strategies on the temperate coast of central Chile: the resident triplefin Helcogrammoides chilensis and the transient kyphosid Girella laevifrons. Using otolith microstructure analysis, daily ages, growth patterns, and back-calculated hatch dates were estimated for young-of-the-year individuals collected from rocky intertidal pools between 2010 and 2011. Hatch dates were analyzed in relation to the lunar cycle using circular statistics. Results revealed clear, non-random lunar-related hatching patterns in both species. H. chilensis exhibited two hatching pulses were both high semidiurnal high tides on the full moon, whereas G. laevifrons showed a unimodal lunar pattern with hatching concentrated near the new moon. These contrasting patterns likely reflect species-specific adaptive strategies associated with habitat use, tidal accessibility, larval retention, and predator avoidance. Our findings provide the first comparative evidence of lunar and semi-lunar recruitment periodicity in resident and transient intertidal fishes from the southeastern Pacific and highlight the role of life-history traits in shaping early life-history timing in temperate rocky shore ecosystems.
